views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Let the already-announced 25 percent List 1 tariffs on about $34B of Chinese goods take effect on July 6 as scheduled, keep List 2 (about $16B) on its public-comment track, and do not yet implement the contingent $200B/10 percent tranche. Do not reopen the May purchase-only package and do not offer a rollback. Hold the current posture for a short observation window, keep a channel open for talks that address the Section 301 structural findings (IP, forced tech transfer), and use farm-support tools only as a backstop if soybean-market damage becomes acute.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Net threat is mixed, closer to unclear than to a high-cost shock or a clear opportunity. The Section 301 record (2018-03-22) documents unreasonable Chinese IP/tech-transfer practices; Beijing still has not offered structural concessions (2017-11-08 commercial MOUs; 2018-05-19 purchase pledge that the White House correctly treated as insufficient on 2018-05-29). The US real economy is not yet paying a material price: industrial production is up to 103.36, Michigan sentiment remains high at 97.9, and VIX is only 16.14. China is showing more strain (CNY to 6.64/6.72). That is leverage. The offset is real: China will match $34B on July 6, targeting soybeans (about $12-14B), autos, and seafood; futures already sold off and farm income was already halved over five years. IMPCH has jumped to $47.0B, consistent with front-running rather than collapse. Escalating immediately to the $200B list would convert a targeted 301 action into a broader consumer/supply-chain tax, invite non-tariff Chinese counters the US cannot easily match, and deepen farm-belt political damage before List 1 has even been observed. Rolling back would throw away the only instrument that collapsed the hollow May truce. Holding first tranche on, $200B kept as contingent leverage, talks only on structural IP is the right stance when leverage and farm-belt costs roughly offset.
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer findings remain unmet; May 19 purchase truce collapsed on 2018-05-29
List 1 $34B / 25 percent is locked for 2018-07-06 with China matching on soy, autos, seafood
US macro still firm (IP 103.36, UMCSENT 97.9); China FX already weakening (CNY about 6.64 to 6.72)
Farm-belt exposure is the main US cost: about $12-14B soy to China, futures already down, incomes pre-weak
$200B/10 percent threat is useful leverage but premature to fire before observing List 1 and China non-tariff options
ZTE denial order showed firm-level US leverage; the June fine/monitor deal already spent some of that chip

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR Section 301 report finds China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable; Trump directs tariffs, WTO case, and investment restrictions.
Joint statement: China agrees to significantly increase purchases; Mnuchin says trade war is on hold.
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25 percent tariffs on about $50B. Truce collapses.
USTR final two-stage $50B plan: 25 percent on List 1 about $34B effective July 6; China announces matching retaliation the same day.
Trump directs USTR to identify an additional about $200B of Chinese imports for 10 percent tariffs if China retaliates against the $50B action.
US industrial production latest 103.36 (2018-07-01), up about 1.6 percent over the window; no trade-war production break yet.
Michigan consumer sentiment 97.9 (2018-07-01), still high; only a modest dip from 99.7.
CNY/USD weakened to 6.6368 on 2018-07-03 from about 6.28 in late March, accelerating after the June 15 tariff lists.
US goods imports from China rose to $47.0B (2018-07-01) from $39.0B in February; front-running, not import collapse.
China 25 percent tariffs on about $34B from July 6 cover soy, corn, wheat, cotton, beef, pork; US sold about $14B soy to China last year.
China matching list starts July 6 on soy, EVs, seafood; aircraft dropped; US $200B/10 percent identified if China proceeds.
Commerce deal to lift ZTE denial order for $1B fine, board/management change, and US compliance monitors.
